item.title: ProxCenter vs PegaProx vs Proxmox Datacenter Manager: Which Multi-Cluster Console Wins in 2026?
item.description:
ProxCenter vs PegaProx vs Proxmox Datacenter Manager: Which Multi-Cluster Console Wins in 2026?

You can run one Proxmox VE node from its built-in web UI forever. The moment you own three clusters in two racks — plus a Proxmox Backup Server — that same UI becomes a tab-hopping exercise in copy-pasting VMIDs. The stock interface has no concept of “all my infrastructure.” It shows one cluster at a time, and it shows it well, but it never shows you the whole estate.

item.title: Scanopy vs Homelable vs Neko-Master: Self-Hosted Network Diagrams That Update Themselves (2026)
item.description: Every network diagram is a lie within about three weeks. You draw the VLANs, label the switch ports, screenshot it into the wiki — and then someone adds a Proxmox node, a test SSID appears on the AP, and the drawing becomes archaeology. Three self-hosted projects are attacking that decay from different directions: Scanopy (5,909 stars), Homelable (4,549) and Neko-Master (4,211) — one scans your subnets and redraws itself, one gives you a curated map with live status, and one turns raw traffic into a geographic picture of what your network is actually doing.

item.title: Self-Hosted Label Printing in 2026: Brother QL vs Niimbot vs Zebra ZPL — Stop Fighting Printer Drivers
item.description: The moment you own 200 physical assets, the label problem stops being cute. You buy a thermal label printer, plug it into a Linux box, and discover that the vendor driver does not exist for your architecture, the “page size” settings are wrong by two millimetres, and every barcode you print is unreadable at 45°.

item.title: Linux Kiosk Mode in 2026: Cage vs Cog vs Porteus Kiosk Compared
item.description: A kiosk is not a computer with a fullscreen browser. A kiosk is an appliance, and the moment a visitor can reach a shell, open a file manager, or press Ctrl+Alt+F2 into a login prompt, you no longer have a kiosk — you have an unattended Linux machine on your lobby floor with your network credentials in its keyring.

item.title: Dokploy vs Komodo vs Arcane in 2026: The Self-Hosted Docker Control Panel Showdown
item.description: Portainer taught a generation of sysadmins that a browser tab is sometimes all the tooling you need. But the 2026 generation of Docker control panels has quietly moved past “browse containers and click restart” — the new contenders do GitOps, multi-server rollouts, database backups, and deployment orchestration. Three projects dominate the conversation right now, and all three shipped releases in the last few weeks: Dokploy (37,702 stars, v0.30.8), Komodo (12,643 stars, v2.3.3), and Arcane (7,764 stars, v2.15.1).

item.title: Self-Hosted KVM Web Management: WebVirtCloud vs Kimchi vs Cockpit Machines
item.description:
Introduction

Managing KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) hosts through the command line is powerful but becomes unwieldy as your virtualization footprint grows. A web-based management interface gives you visibility into all your VMs, enables team collaboration, and provides point-and-click provisioning without SSH-ing into each host. This guide compares three leading open-source KVM web management platforms: WebVirtCloud, Kimchi, and Cockpit Machines.

item.title: Self-Hosted Linux Power Management Analysis: powertop vs powerstat vs turbostat Guide
item.description:
Introduction

Server power consumption directly impacts your electricity bill, cooling requirements, and hardware lifespan. For homelab operators and data center administrators alike, understanding exactly where your system draws power — and how to reduce it — is essential for cost-effective operations. Linux provides several powerful command-line tools for power analysis, each designed for different use cases.

item.title: Self-Hosted Linux Device Management: systemd-udevd vs eudev vs mdev (2026)
item.description: Linux device management is the unsung hero of every self-hosted infrastructure. When you plug in a USB drive, insert a PCIe card, or attach a network interface, the device manager is what creates the device nodes, sets permissions, and triggers the actions that make hardware usable. For self-hosted server administrators managing bare-metal infrastructure, homelab setups, or container hosts with GPU passthrough, choosing the right device management framework directly impacts system reliability, boot time, and device hot-plug behavior.

item.title: Self-Hosted IP-KVM Solutions: PiKVM vs TinyPilot vs BliKVM
item.description: Managing bare-metal servers remotely requires out-of-band access — the ability to control a machine even when its operating system is unresponsive. IP-KVM (IP-based Keyboard-Video-Mouse) solutions provide remote console access by capturing video output and injecting keyboard/mouse input over the network. This guide compares three popular open-source IP-KVM platforms: PiKVM, TinyPilot, and BliKVM.

item.title: Self-Hosted mDNS Reflector: Avahi vs mdns-reflector vs bonjour-reflector (2026)
item.description: In modern networked environments, service discovery protocols like mDNS (Multicast DNS) and DNS-SD (DNS Service Discovery) allow devices to find each other without a central directory server. Apple calls this Bonjour; the open-source implementation is Avahi. The problem? mDNS is a link-local protocol — it does not cross VLAN or subnet boundaries by design.

item.title: Self-Hosted Network Device Discovery: WatchYourLAN vs NetAlertX vs Pi.Alert (2026)
item.description: When managing a homelab, small business network, or enterprise LAN, knowing every device on your network is critical for security and operations. Unrecognized devices can indicate unauthorized access, compromised endpoints, or simply shadow IT that needs to be documented. Three open-source projects specialize in this problem: WatchYourLAN, NetAlertX, and Pi.Alert. Each uses ARP scanning as its primary discovery mechanism but differs significantly in features, deployment, and alerting capabilities.

item.title: Homer vs Heimdall vs Flame: Best Self-Hosted Startpage Dashboard 2026
item.description: If you run a homelab or self-host multiple services, you know the frustration of managing a growing list of URLs, ports, and bookmarks. Every new container or application adds another address to remember. A self-hosted startpage dashboard solves this permanently: a single landing page that organizes all your services, shows their status, and becomes your browser’s home page.

item.title: Proxmox VE vs XCP-ng vs oVirt: Best Self-Hosted Virtualization Platform 2026
item.description: If you’re running servers at home or in a small organization, relying on VMware ESXi with its restrictive licensing or paying per-socket fees for Hyper-V is no longer the only option. Open source virtualization platforms have matured significantly, offering enterprise-grade features with full transparency and zero licensing costs.

item.title: Self-Hosted Kubernetes: k3s vs k0s vs Talos Linux — Best Lightweight K8s Distros 2026
item.description: Running Kubernetes at home used to mean provisioning a full cluster with kubeadm — multiple control-plane nodes, etcd backups, manual CNI setup, and hours of configuration. That changed with the rise of lightweight Kubernetes distributions designed specifically for edge computing, homelabs, and self-hosted workloads.
